facts: I estimate that I started using AI for programming six to twelve months before the original interview.
At work a Teams channel and working group help us obtain access to new AI models, additional tokens and advice on AI use.
Our company intranet maintains a whitelist of permitted AI tools.

For general office work my company uses Microsoft Copilot 365 for Teams meeting transcription, Excel data, email drafts and Word summaries. We also have an internally hosted translation model instead of Google Translate.

For development we mainly use GitHub Copilot and Open Code, an open-source alternative similar to the tool transcribed as Cloud Code. A Cloud Code pilot is underway but it is not yet an official announced tool; I expect it may become available later.
For Android development I use Gemini integrated into Android Studio, although I said it was not officially whitelisted by my company. Its capability at the time was limited to advanced autocomplete.
GitHub Copilot is integrated into Visual Studio Code at work.

AI is always integrated into my IDE and usually runs in the background. In chat mode it acts as an agent; in code mode it provides advanced autocomplete so well integrated that I sometimes cannot distinguish it from ordinary autocomplete.

I use AI to explain design patterns and unfamiliar code, build proofs of concept that I review and refine or rewrite with AI assistance, and implement well-defined functions such as a Fibonacci-number function. I describe this as agentic engineering, using AI to implement my ideas.
I often use AI for writing and generating code.
I sometimes use AI for debugging.
I often use AI to understand unfamiliar code.
I sometimes use AI for refactoring.
I often use AI to write tests.
I often use AI to write documentation.
I sometimes use AI for explaining concepts and learning; I am still not accustomed to AI teaching me things.
One of my most recent AI-assisted programming tasks was improving code quality in an existing project.

For the existing project's code-quality task, which had no AI integration yet, I opened my IDE, cloned the project using Git, started GitHub Copilot and selected Opus, the most expensive model available to us, to generate an agent Markdown file.
I asked Opus to examine the project code and document its purpose, dependencies, common patterns and tools in an agent Markdown file to assist future agentic development.

Opus took about twenty to thirty minutes on the relatively small project to create an agent Markdown file that could supply project context for future changes. I then switched to a cheaper model, transcribed as Cloud Sonnet 4.6.

I supplied the cheaper AI model with issues found in logs and SonarQube, including code coverage, vulnerabilities and bad practices. It fixed issues individually. I opened several pull requests step by step, ensured tests and code-quality CI checks passed, combined changes into one release and asked QA to test them together because they mostly affected quality rather than behavior and separate testing would take too long.
The AI-assisted code-quality improvement workflow I described took place the day before the original interview.
The recent code-quality task was purely technical. Our company has compliance thresholds for code quality and security.

When code quality or security falls below compliance thresholds, DevOps and architecture teams ask developers to improve quality, add missing tests or fix vulnerabilities. I initiated my recent task proactively; otherwise DevOps and security would eventually escalate it through frequent compliance checks.
The recent AI-assisted code-quality improvement task took approximately four hours.
In my general working day I write code often.
In my general working day I review code often.
I rated writing and reviewing code often rather than very often because I am officially an engineering manager, not a line developer.
I often do bug fixing and debugging in my general work.
I often do testing because coding, reviewing, debugging and testing usually come together. I sometimes work on specifications.
In my general work I sometimes do documentation.
I conservatively rated continuous learning as rare in my general working day.
Of my frequently performed development activities, debugging usually takes the most time.
A recent debugging example involved an application displaying notifications that had already been marked as seen.

Previously seen notifications should not reappear in the notification dropdown. Although the client sent the notification ID to the backend to mark it as read, the backend failed to record this and notifications reappeared after restart. I worked on the client side and needed a backend developer to help identify and fix the root cause.
My first step in the notification bug was debugging to identify the behavior, not contacting another developer.
After debugging the client side of the notification issue, I contacted a developer responsible for the other part of the system because I could not identify the problem on my side.
I identified the backend developer's change as the point after which the notification task was successfully completed; the source does not specify a separate verification procedure here.
I often work with code I did not write, because teams take over services after organizational changes and our system contains legacy code predating my or my teammates' employment.

For the notification issue I used little AI. Knowing the application structure, I identified and read the notification module, used Chrome DevTools to inspect network calls and rendered component classes and IDs in the DOM, identified the React component and traced it back to the network-call code. This was manual debugging.

I also act as an application publisher, releasing apps to Google Play and Apple App Store. While doing less attention-intensive work I used GitHub Copilot in the background to build a dashboard of our apps.

I wanted one dashboard for iOS and Android releases, countries of availability and installation counts instead of logging into two systems. Through iterative prompting, vibe coding and context engineering I obtained it, and I provided authentication credentials securely with limited access rights.

I began the dashboard task with a large prompt requesting a frontend and backend aggregating Google Play Developer API and Apple Developer data for production apps, versions and countries. I instructed AI to ask about uncertain requirements; it asked about secret handling, displayed information and layout during implementation.
Without AI I would have started the dashboard by identifying dependencies and designing the application's internal logic.

Without AI I would have needed to read Google Developer and Apple Developer or Apple Connect API documentation. AI did that for me. Since the dashboard was not a production application, I prioritized obtaining the data over code quality.
I estimate the dashboard would have taken me several days to build manually, so AI saved considerable time.
When writing code manually, unlike the AI-generated dashboard workflow, I usually establish high-level tests as I develop to ensure functionality remains intact.
For the dashboard AI chose tools and libraries unfamiliar to me, unlike my normal development choices. Building it myself would likely have required my manager's approval because of the time needed.
I characterized my current method for deciding whether to rely on AI output as basic.
I constantly review AI work, particularly production applications using client data, and provide good agent context through agent Markdown or skill files.
I believe defining reusable AI skills for test writing, data anonymization or UI verification and referencing them improves quality. Humans remain accountable for AI output.
I believe AI-generated output must be validated by the human using it.

I try to validate AI output continuously. Even for my nonproduction dashboard I read the code to check for malicious or unintended behavior, such as POST requests changing data through Apple or Google APIs.
I also checked the generated dashboard code for anything obviously wrong.
I had no further specific interview comments, but noted that even developers at the leading edge of AI use are continually experimenting with it.
Developers are continually discovering AI workflows and quality-control patterns, with new approaches and tools appearing weekly. I cautioned that my answers might differ a month or two later.
